title: Stage 3: Bad data
summary: Survive malformed rows: reject each one with a line number and a reason, without a single exception.

steps.title: Real input is dirty
body: So far every line was perfect. Real exports are not. People leave columns out, type `abc` where a number goes, invent categories, and paste dates in the wrong format:
A good tool does not fall over, and it does not quietly drop the bad lines either. It keeps everything it can read and **says exactly what was wrong with the rest, and where**:
The line numbers are the ones a person would see in a text editor: the header is line 1, and blank lines count. That is what lets someone open the file and fix it.

steps.prompt: Your stage 2 program is given 500 lines. Line 317 has `abc` as its amount. What happens?
options: `decimal.Parse` throws, the program crashes, and nothing is reported for any of the 500 lines
Line 317 is skipped and the other 499 are reported
Line 317 is reported with an amount of 0.00
The program reports the first 316 lines and then stops
steps.explain: `Parse` throws a `FormatException` on bad text. Nothing catches it, so the program dies inside the reading loop, before it has printed a single line. One typo costs the whole report.

steps.title: A bad row is a result, not an exception
body: You could wrap the parsing in `try`/`catch`. But a malformed line in an export is not a surprise. It is one of the two things you **expect** from every line: either it is an expense, or it is rejected for a reason. When failure is part of the job, put it in the return type.
A small family of records says it exactly:
record Rejected(int LineNumber, string Reason) : ParseResult;

`ParseResult` is `abstract`: you can never create a bare one. Every `ParseResult` is a `Parsed` carrying an expense, or a `Rejected` carrying the line number and the reason. There is no third state, and no `null` to forget about.
The parser returns one or the other, and the caller sorts them with `is`:
Nothing is thrown, nothing is caught, and the loop carries on to the next line.

steps.prompt: Complete the result types and the code that uses them.
steps.explain: Both records inherit from `ParseResult`, so a method can return either. `is Parsed parsed` tests the type and gives you a variable of that type in one step.

steps.title: Line numbers, and a smarter Split
body: To report *where* a row went wrong, count lines as you read them. Count **every** line, before any is skipped, so the number matches what a person sees in an editor:
Two more things real data does. Descriptions contain commas (`Hotel, one night`), and people put spaces around values. `Split` has options for both:
- The `4` means *at most four pieces*. After the third comma the rest of the line stays together, so `Hotel, one night` survives as one description.
- `TrimEntries` removes the spaces around each piece.
A line with too few commas gives fewer than four pieces. That is the first thing to check, **before** you touch `parts[2]`.

steps.title: Reject short rows
prompt: Make the program survive rows with missing columns.
1. Add the three records from the card: `ParseResult`, `Parsed(Expense Expense)` and `Rejected(int LineNumber, string Reason)`.
2. Count line numbers in the reading loop. Every line counts, including the header and blank lines.

3. Replace `ParseExpense` with `ParseResult ParseLine(int lineNumber, string line)`. Split with `line.Split(',', 4, StringSplitOptions.TrimEntries)`. If there are not exactly 4 parts, return a `Rejected` with the reason `expected 4 columns but found N`. Otherwise parse as before and return a `Parsed`.
4. Keep two lists: the expenses, and the `Rejected` results.
Print the valid expenses as before, then `Valid:` (it replaces `Expenses:`), `Total:`, `Rejected:` and one indented line per rejected row. For this input:
Each rejected line is two spaces, `line N: `, then the reason. With nothing rejected, print `Rejected: 0` and stop.
starter: return new Expense(date, category, amount, parts[3]);
enum Category { Travel, Meals, Lodging, Supplies, Other }
record Expense(DateOnly Date, Category Category, decimal Amount, string Description);
solution: return new Rejected(lineNumber, $"expected 4 columns but found {parts.Length}");
return new Parsed(new Expense(date, category, amount, parts[3]));
enum Category { Travel, Meals, Lodging, Supplies, Other }

hints: Start with the types at the bottom of the file, then change the loop: `lineNumber++` must be the first statement inside it.

In `ParseLine`: `if (parts.Length != 4) return new Rejected(lineNumber, $"expected 4 columns but found {parts.Length}");`. The happy path ends with `return new Parsed(new Expense(date, category, amount, parts[3]));`.
After the loop: `foreach (var rejection in rejected) Console.WriteLine($"  line {rejection.LineNumber}: {rejection.Reason}");`

steps.title: TryParse: ask, don't catch
body: Every `Parse` method has a `TryParse` twin. It returns `false` instead of throwing, and hands the value back through an `out` parameter:
// from here on, amount is a real decimal

Notice the shape: test for the problem, return early, and carry on with a value you can trust. A method built from these **guard clauses** reads straight down the page, one check per column, with the success case on the last line.
Dates work the same way. The exact-format version takes one more argument, `DateTimeStyles.None`, which means *no special allowances*:
if (!DateOnly.TryParseExact(parts[0], "yyyy-MM-dd", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, DateTimeStyles.None, out var date))
It rejects text in another format, and also dates that do not exist, such as `2026-02-30`.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into a parser built from guard clauses. Check the column count before reading any column, and put the success case last.
steps.explain: Each guard protects the lines below it. Reading `parts[2]` before checking the length would crash on a short row, which is the very thing the method exists to prevent.

steps.title: Reject bad dates and amounts
prompt: `ParseLine` still crashes on `abc`. Replace the two risky `Parse` calls with guard clauses.
After the column check, in this order:
- if the first column is not a real date in `yyyy-MM-dd` form, reject with `invalid date 'TEXT'`,
- if the third column is not a number, reject with `invalid amount 'TEXT'`,
where `TEXT` is the column's text in single quotes. Report only the **first** problem on a line. Leave the category as it is for now. For this input:

tests.name: short row, bad amount, bad date

hints: Each check has the same shape: `if (!Something.TryParse(..., out var value)) return new Rejected(lineNumber, ...);`
The date check is `DateOnly.TryParseExact(parts[0], "yyyy-MM-dd", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, DateTimeStyles.None, out var date)`.
The amount check is `decimal.TryParse(parts[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out var amount)` and its reason is `$"invalid amount '{parts[2]}'"`.

steps.title: Two traps in Enum.TryParse
body: `Enum.TryParse<Category>(text, out var category)` has two behaviours that surprise almost everyone.
**It is case-sensitive.** `"meals"` fails, although any person would accept it. Pass `ignoreCase: true`:
Enum.TryParse<Category>("meals", ignoreCase: true, out var category)   // true, Category.Meals

**It accepts numbers.** An enum is a number underneath, so `"7"` parses successfully into a `Category` with the value 7, which has no name and means nothing. `Enum.IsDefined` asks whether a value is one of the declared members:
if (!Enum.TryParse<Category>(parts[1], ignoreCase: true, out var category) || !Enum.IsDefined(category))
Parsing proves the text is a number. It does not prove the number makes sense. An amount of `-5.00` parses perfectly well, and is still not an expense.

code: bool parsed = Enum.TryParse<Category>("7", out var category);
steps.explain: `TryParse` happily turns `"7"` into `(Category)7`. Only `IsDefined` notices that no member has that value.

steps.title: Reject unknown categories and bad amounts
prompt: Finish the validation. Two more guard clauses:

- between the date check and the amount check: if the second column is not one of the `Category` names, reject with `unknown category 'TEXT'`. Upper and lower case do not matter (`meals` is `Meals`), but a number such as `7` is not a category.
- last of all: if the amount is zero or negative, reject with `amount must be positive`.
The checks run in column order: columns, date, category, amount, positive. For this input:
After this step no input, however broken, should crash the program.
